papers.ed_link: ED assessment of children presenting with suspected severe malaria

clinical.rationale: Provides new age-based creatinine and urea thresholds that can improve ED risk stratification of children with severe malaria.

research.rationale: Large IPD meta-analysis using Bayesian spline models to derive age-specific prognostic thresholds, a method uncommon in PEM research.

papers.one_line: In severe malaria, creatinine >3 times age-predicted baseline or urea >10 mmol/L identifies children at high risk of death.

summary.why_it_matters: Current severe malaria AKI thresholds are based on adult values and miss many children; ED-usable age-based criteria could improve risk stratification.
summary.design: Individual patient data meta-analysis of 22,663 patients from 14 prospective severe malaria studies, using Bayesian penalised spline models with age interactions.
summary.key_findings: Among 16,441 included patients, 84% were children under 15. Admission creatinine >3 times age/weight-predicted baseline and urea >10 mmol/L were associated with >5% mortality. In children, urea predicted death better than creatinine and correlated with parasite biomass. The new thresholds identify 4-8 times more children with severe malaria AKI at high risk of death.
summary.bottom_line: ED clinicians should use age-based creatinine fold-change or a urea threshold of 10 mmol/L, rather than adult absolute values, to recognize severe malaria AKI in children.

papers.ed_link: children with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest managed by bystanders and EMS

clinical.rationale: Large national registry data support rescue-breathing CPR over compression-only CPR for pediatric OHCA, reinforcing current pediatric resuscitation guidance.

research.rationale: Standard registry analysis with temporal trend modeling and modified Poisson regression; robust but not methodologically novel.

papers.one_line: In Japanese children with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, rescue-breathing bystander CPR was associated with better neurologically favorable survival than compression-only CPR.

summary.why_it_matters: This large national study challenges the idea that compression-only CPR is enough for children, showing that adding rescue breaths was linked to better survival and neurologic outcomes after pediatric cardiac arrest.
summary.design: Retrospective cohort study using the nationwide All-Japan Utstein Registry, including 26,785 children aged 17 years or younger with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest from 2005 to 2023.
summary.key_findings: Compression-only CPR rose from 14.6% in 2005 to 55.1% in 2023, while rescue-breathing CPR fell from 41.7% to 10.4%; the proportion receiving no bystander CPR plateaued around 35% after 2013. Neurologically favorable 30-day survival was 3.6% with no bystander CPR, 9.5% with compression-only CPR, and 16.0% with rescue-breathing CPR. Compared with compression-only CPR, rescue-breathing CPR was associated with higher rates of neurologically favorable survival (adjusted RR 1.71), 30-day survival (1.51), and prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (1.62).
summary.bottom_line: Rescue breathing remains important in pediatric resuscitation, even as compression-only CPR has become more common.

papers.methods_note: Nationwide prospective registry cohort with multinomial logistic regression and modified Poisson regression.

clinical.rationale: Population-level cross-sectional study of ED and outpatient mental health visits; provides background on inequities but no direct clinical decision.

research.rationale: Novel linkage of climate vulnerability and historical redlining to pediatric mental health utilization; standard cross-sectional design.

papers.one_line: Children in climate-vulnerable, historically redlined neighborhoods had higher rates of mental health-related ED and outpatient visits.

summary.why_it_matters: This study links climate vulnerability and historical redlining to children's mental health care use, showing that structural inequities may compound climate-related stress in marginalized neighborhoods.
summary.design: Cross-sectional study using New York State all-payer hospital data from 2017 to 2022 for children under 18, with census-tract-level analysis of climate vulnerability, redlining status, and mental health visits.
summary.key_findings: Among 553,134 mental health visits (mean age 7.2 years; 51.6% male), children in the highest climate-vulnerability areas had higher outpatient visit rates than those in the lowest (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.72-2.27), while ED rates were not significantly higher (RR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.96-1.35). In historically redlined neighborhoods, high vulnerability was associated with increased outpatient (RR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.44-1.51) and ED (RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.09) use; in nonredlined areas, outpatient use was lower (RR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.45-0.49).
summary.bottom_line: Children living in historically redlined, climate-vulnerable neighborhoods have higher mental health care utilization, highlighting geographic and structural disparities relevant to climate preparedness and mental health services.

papers.methods_note: Cross-sectional analysis of New York State all-payer hospital administrative data (2017-2022) with census-tract-level Poisson regression.
